O tell her, Swallow, thou that knowest each, That bright and fierce and fickle is the South, And dark and true and tender is the North.

O Swallow, Swallow, if I could follow, and light Upon her lattice, I would pipe and trill, And cheep and twitter twenty million loves.

O were I thou that she might take me in, And lay me on her bosom, and her heart Would rock the snowy cradle till I died.

Why lingereth she to clothe her heart with love, Delaying as the tender ash delays To clothe herself, when all the woods are green?

O tell her, Swallow, that thy brood is flown: Say to her, I do but wanton in the South, But in the North long since my nest is made.

O tell her, brief is life but love is long, And brief the sun of summer in the North, And brief the moon of beauty in the South.

O Swallow, flying from the golden woods, Fly to her, and pipe and woo her, and make her mine, And tell her, tell her, that I follow thee.

references.quote: go south in the winter.
O swallow swallow

tiresias.title: Tiresias, the Blind Seer
tiresias.body_html:
In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Book III, Tiresias has lived as both man and woman. Asked to judge a dispute between Jupiter and Juno about sexual pleasure, he answers Jupiter; Juno blinds him, and Jupiter compensates him with prophetic knowledge. Eliot quotes this episode in his note.

Eliot calls Tiresias the poem's most important personage and says the sexes meet in him. Watching the typist and clerk, the seer carries ancient knowledge into an ordinary modern room. His foresight provides no rescue: the encounter repeats what he has already suffered. The note's claim that he unites the figures offers a connection among their fragments without making their experiences identical.

references.quote:
I Tiresias, though blind, throbbing between two lives,
  Old man with wrinkled female breasts, can see
  At the violet hour, the evening hour that strives
  Homeward, and brings the sailor home from sea,
  The typist home at teatime, clears her breakfast, lights
  Her stove, and lays out food in tins.
  Out of the window perilously spread
  Her drying combinations touched by the sun’s last rays,
  On the divan are piled (at night her bed)
  Stockings, slippers, camisoles, and stays.
  I Tiresias, old man with wrinkled dugs
  Perceived the scene, and foretold the rest—
  I too awaited the expected guest.
  He, the young man carbuncular, arrives,
  A small house agent’s clerk, with one bold stare,
  One of the low on whom assurance sits
  As a silk hat on a Bradford millionaire.
  The time is now propitious, as he guesses,
  The meal is ended, she is bored and tired,
  Endeavours to engage her in caresses
  Which still are unreproved, if undesired.
  Flushed and decided, he assaults at once;
  Exploring hands encounter no defence;
  His vanity requires no response,
  And makes a welcome of indifference.
  (And I Tiresias have foresuffered all
  Enacted on this same divan or bed;
  I who have sat by Thebes below the wall
  And walked among the lowest of the dead.)
  Bestows one final patronising kiss,
  And gropes his way, finding the stairs unlit . . .

tristan.title: Wagner's Tristan and Isolde
tristan.body_html:
Eliot's notes identify two quotations from Wagner's Tristan und Isolde. In Act I, a sailor's song calls toward an absent Irish girl across the sea. In Act III, the sea is described as desolate and empty while the dying Tristan waits for Isolde's arrival.

The German passages enclose the hyacinth-garden memory. An opening call of desire is answered by a sea emptied of the awaited figure. The garden's inability to speak therefore stands between musical voices of longing and absence, allowing romantic intensity and emotional failure to occupy the same remembered moment.

references.quote:
Frisch weht der Wind
       Der Heimat zu
       Mein Irisch Kind,
       Wo weilest du?
Oed’ und leer das Meer.

upanishad.title: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
upanishad.body_html:
The thunder's three instructions come from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, in the story commonly numbered 5.2. Eliot's note gives 5.1 and translates the imperatives as giving, sympathizing, and controlling. In the story, gods, human beings, and demons hear the same syllable, “Da,” as the particular instruction each needs. A translation with the Sanskrit passage sets out these different hearings.

Eliot rearranges the commands as Datta, Dayadhvam, Damyata, giving each a separate human scene. A single sound becomes several ethical demands. After so many quotations whose speakers cannot reach one another, thunder supplies a shared utterance that still requires each listener to interpret and act.

references.quote:
DA
  Datta: what have we given?
  My friend, blood shaking my heart
  The awful daring of a moment’s surrender
  Which an age of prudence can never retract
  By this, and this only, we have existed
  Which is not to be found in our obituaries
  Or in memories draped by the beneficent spider
  Or under seals broken by the lean solicitor
  In our empty rooms
  DA
  Dayadhvam: I have heard the key
  Turn in the door once and turn once only
  We think of the key, each in his prison
  Thinking of the key, each confirms a prison
  Only at nightfall, aetherial rumours
  Revive for a moment a broken Coriolanus
  DA
  Damyata: The boat responded
  Gaily, to the hand expert with sail and oar
  The sea was calm, your heart would have responded
  Gaily, when invited, beating obedient
  To controlling hands
Datta. Dayadhvam. Damyata.

verlaine.title: Verlaine's Parsifal
verlaine.body_html:
Eliot's note identifies Paul Verlaine's poem Parsifal as the source of the French line about children's voices singing in a dome. Verlaine's poem invokes the Grail world associated with Parsifal and brings its spiritual drama toward a musical, sacred conclusion.

Eliot places the line immediately after the song about Mrs Porter and her daughter washing their feet. A sacred musical space suddenly opens within the bawdy river passage. The juxtaposition can suggest purification or expose the distance between ritual promise and modern life; the poem leaves both tones audible.

references.quote: Et O ces voix d’enfants, chantant dans la coupole!

webster.title: John Webster's The White Devil
webster.body_html:
John Webster's The White Devil supplies the burial song Eliot recalls at the end of Part I. In Webster, the wolf is to be kept from the grave because it may dig up the body; Eliot changes the animal into the dog, supposedly humanity's friend. His notes also connect the wind at the door and the later image of the spider over memorials with Webster.

These scraps carry the Jacobean tragedy's atmosphere of murder, insecure burial, and mourning into modern conversation. Even friendship cannot guarantee the dead their rest. The later thought that people will quickly remarry turns private remembrance into another fragile defence against time.

references.quote:
“Oh keep the Dog far hence, that’s friend to men,
  “Or with his nails he’ll dig it up again!
The wind under the door.
the grass is singing

weston.title: Jessie Weston: From Ritual to Romance
weston.body_html:
In his opening note, Eliot acknowledges Jessie L. Weston's From Ritual to Romance as a source for the poem's title, plan, and much of its incidental symbolism. Weston connects medieval Grail narratives with fertility ritual, stressing relations among an injured ruler, an afflicted land, and a quest for restoration.

Her account helps connect the Fisher King, fishing, drought, the dangerous chapel, and the final effort to put one's lands in order. It is a source Eliot used, rather than an established explanation of all Grail traditions or a master key to every passage. In the poem, the promised restoration remains surrounded by competing voices and incomplete acts.

references.quote:
Over the tumbled graves, about the chapel
  There is the empty chapel, only the wind’s home.

whitman.title: Walt Whitman, Lilacs, and the Hermit Thrush
whitman.body_html:
The lilacs invite comparison with Walt Whitman's elegy When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd. Whitman's poem joins returning spring, the mourning of Lincoln, and a hermit thrush whose song helps the speaker confront death. The poem itself develops these images across an extended act of remembrance.

A more direct correspondence appears in the hermit-thrush passage at lines 357–358, within the earlier evocation of a landscape without water:

Here is no water but only rock […] Where the hermit-thrush sings in the pine trees Drip drop drip drop drop drop drop But there is no water

The apparent dripping comes from the hermit thrush's song. Eliot's own note to line 357 specifically celebrates its “water-dripping song.” He recalls hearing the bird in Quebec County and cites Frank Chapman's Handbook of Birds of Eastern North America on its secluded woodland habitat and the purity and sweetness of its tone. In the dry mountain landscape, the song briefly makes an imagined spring audible, before the blunt reminder that there is no water. It awakens the sensation of relief without supplying the water the exhausted travellers need.

The hermit thrush is also a central image in Whitman's elegy:

Solitary the thrush, The hermit withdrawn to himself, avoiding the settlements, Sings by himself a song.

Whitman ultimately brings the lilac, the star, and the bird's song together in remembrance of the dead. Eliot's lilacs emerge painfully from dead land, while his later thrush seems to sing water into a landscape that has none. The connection to Whitman remains an interpretive echo, rather than an attribution Eliot makes in his notes. Where Whitman gathers these images into a sustained mourning song, Eliot lets them return as scattered, troubled reminders of the desire for consolation.

references.quote: Lilacs

Where the hermit-thrush sings in the pine trees
  Drip drop drip drop drop drop drop
